title: NASCAR Daytona takeaways: Ryan Preece seizes last Chase spot with stunning win
content:
DAYTONA BEACH, Fla. — NASCAR’s new playoff system seemingly eliminated the “win and in” scenario to make the Chase.

Ryan Preece proved otherwise.

Preece scored his first career NASCAR Cup Series victory when he needed it the most, a last-gasp win Saturday at Daytona International Speedway that saved his season and put him into the 16-driver Chase over Shane van Gisbergen.

“I’m just speechless right now,” said an elated Preece, who drives for RFK Racing. “We’re fighters. When you put our back against the wall, we swing hard.”

On the white flag lap of overtime, Zane Smith was leading Preece and Daytona 500 winner Tyler Reddick. But when Smith and Reddick made contact, it allowed Preece to take the lead on the bottom lane.

As more cars wrecked behind the incident, NASCAR was forced to throw the caution flag — freezing the field with Preece in front.

The bonus points for a win eliminated van Gisbergen, who had a 31-point lead over Preece entering the regular-season finale.

“One night doesn’t sum up our year,” van Gisbergen said. “It’s been cool to be close. Shame we’re not in it.”

From 2014 to 2025, NASCAR used a “win and in” playoff format, where a single race victory guaranteed a driver’s place in the playoffs. This season, NASCAR returned to a similar version of its old “Chase” playoff format, doing away with the “win and in” in favor of season-long points accumulation to determine the field.

Still, Preece effectively brought back the old format for one night, needing a big performance and for van Gisbergen to struggle to have a chance. Van Gisbergen, the road-course ace with seven victories the past two seasons, finished 27th.

The 16-driver field for NASCAR’s Chase is: Denny Hamlin, Ryan Blaney, Ty Gibbs, Tyler Reddick, Christopher Bell, Chase Briscoe, Kyle Larson, Chase Elliott, Joey Logano, Chris Buescher, Carson Hocevar, William Byron, Daniel Suárez, Bubba Wallace, Austin Cindric and Preece.

In Aug. 2023, Preece suffered one of the most frightening crashes in recent NASCAR history on the backstretch at Daytona. His car caught the grass and flipped over and over, twirling through the air and smashing multiple times.

Preece knew it could have ended his career — or even his life.

Then he had another airborne crash at Daytona in Feb. 2025 during the Daytona 500, adding a second brutal crash to his history at the track.

To end up in victory lane at the same place, with his first career Cup Series victory at that, and win his way into the Chase when even a second-place drive wouldn’t have been enough, was an incredible feat.

“It’s such a clutch moment for Ryan,” RFK Racing owner Brad Keselowski said. “To drive a great race and go get a win with everything on the line, those are nights you remember.”

— Jeff Gluck

Holding a 31-point lead over Preece, van Gisbergen seemed poised to punch his Chase ticket if he could make it through Daytona unscathed, not an easy thing on a drafting track. That van Gisbergen would advance was only reinforced when he won Stage 1 to add another seven points to his advantage.

So how then did van Gisbergen miss out by 17 points, even though he did make it to the finish with his car in one piece?

One was Preece putting on a determined drive, essentially willing himself to the victory, bullying his way forward after an early spin, culminating with him earning his first-career win. But also not helping van Gisbergen’s cause was a race that ran caution-free for a long stretch, forcing teams to enact various fuel strategies. For van Gisbergen, this meant pitting under caution late, while Preece stayed out — enough of a gap to flip their positions in the standings.

And when van Gisbergen, who dropped to 27th, was never able to move forward over the final two overtime laps, it sealed his fate. Despite two wins, and several strong runs on oval tracks that aren’t his forte, van Gisbergen’s season will not include a spot in the Chase.

“It’s pretty fresh now, but congratulations to Preece,” van Gisbergen said. “One night doesn’t sum up the year for this team. We just weren’t good enough tonight, but it’s been cool to be this close.”

There are a lot of positives to pull from the regular-season for van Gisbergen, whose background is racing on road courses. Still, to some degree it is a tough blow to suffer. Four races ago he held a 57-point lead, only to see it vanish with a succession of subpar finishes that left him vulnerable to a surging Preece.

That’s a lot of points to hemorrhage. And on Saturday night, Preece finally was able to leapfrog the Trackhouse Racing driver.

“I haven’t done a good enough job throughout the year,” van Gisbergen said. “We’ve lost points at various places. We didn’t just lose it tonight.”

— Jordan Bianchi

Team Penske’s Austin Cindric was vulnerable to elimination, but he finished sixth on Saturday night to make the Chase by 26 points over van Gisbergen.

Cindric entered with a 44-point lead over Preece, but the way the racing shook out, there was a moment late in the going when Cindric could have been eliminated based on his track position.

He ended up moving further up the running order while van Gisbergen got caught in the last-lap crash, and Cindric avoided what would have been a total meltdown by surviving with a top-10.

Still, the No. 15 seed knows there’s a lot of work ahead.

“We’ve got to absolutely kill it to think we have a shot at a championship with the way that the points reset,” Cindric said. “But this team is capable of a lot, and I want to see how far we can go.”

— Jeff Gluck
